title: Christine de Pizan
wiki_lead:
Christine de Pizan or Pisan (French: [kʁistin də pizɑ̃] , Middle French: [krisˈtinə də piˈzã]; born Cristina da Pizzano; September 1364 – c. 1430), was a Venetian-born French court writer for King Charles VI of France and several French royal dukes, in both prose and poetry. She wrote in French, having been raised in France to parents who came from Bologna. Her father was invited to the French court in 1368, when Christine was only four years old, to serve as a doctor and astrologer. He insisted that his daughter learn philosophy, Latin, Italian, French, history, literature, and science, which was very unusual for the time.
Christine became a court writer in medieval France after the death of her husband. Her patrons included dukes Louis I of Orleans, Philip the Bold of Burgundy, and his son John the Fearless.  Considered to be some of the earliest feminist writings, her work includes novels, poetry, and biography, and she also penned literary, historical, philosophical, political, and religious reviews and analyses. Her best known works are The Book of the City of Ladies and The Treasure of the City of Ladies, both prose works written when she worked for John the Fearless of Burgundy. Her books of advice to princesses, princes, and knights remained in print until the sixteenth century.

Life


Early life and family (1364–1389)
Christine de Pizan was born in 1364 in the Republic of Venice, Italy. She was the daughter of Tommaso di Benvenuto da Pizzano. Her father became known as Thomas de Pizan, named for the family's origins in the village of Pizzano (currently part of the municipality of Monterenzio), southeast of Bologna. Her father worked as a physician, court astrologer and Councillor of the Republic of Venice. Thomas de Pizan accepted an appointment to the court of Charles V of France as the king's astrologer and in 1368 Christine moved to Paris. In 1379 Christine de Pizan married the notary and royal secretary Etienne du Castel.
She had three children. Her daughter became a nun at the Dominican convent of Poissy in 1397 as a companion to the King's daughter Marie. Christine's husband died of the plague in 1389, a year after her father had died. On 4 June 1389, in a judgment concerning a lawsuit filed against her by the archbishop of Sens and François Chanteprime, councillors of the King, Christine was called "damoiselle" and "widow of Estienne du Castel".


Writing career (1389–1405)
After her husband Etienne died, Christine was left to support her mother and her children.  When she tried to collect money from her husband's estate, she faced complicated lawsuits regarding the recovery of salaries still owed to her husband. Through this, Christine became a court writer. By 1393, she was writing love ballads, which caught the attention of wealthy patrons within the court. Christine became a prolific writer. Her involvement in the production of her books and her skillful use of patronage in turbulent political times has earned her the title of the first professional woman of letters in Europe.

Although Venetian by birth, Christine expressed a fervent nationalism for France. Affectively and financially she became attached to the French royal family, donating or dedicating her early ballads to its members, including Isabeau of Bavaria, Louis I, Duke of Orléans, and Marie of Berry. Patronage changed in the late Middle Ages. Texts were still produced and circulated as continuous roll manuscripts, but were increasingly replaced by the bound codex. Members of the royal family became patrons of writers by commissioning books. As materials became cheaper a book trade developed, so writers and bookmakers produced books for the French nobility, who could afford to establish their own libraries. grok_lead: Christine de Pizan (1364âc. 1430) was an Italian-born writer who lived and worked in France, recognized as the first woman in Europe to earn a living as a professional author by producing commissioned literary works for the royal court and nobility. Born in Venice to a scholar and astrologer appointed to the court of King Charles V, she relocated to Paris as a child, where she received an education uncommon for women of her era, including access to court libraries. Married young to a royal secretary, she was widowed around 1390, leaving her with three children and financial debts that compelled her to turn to writing for sustenance, beginning with poetry and evolving into prose treatises and allegories. Over her career, de Pizan composed more than 40 works, including lyrical ballads expressing personal grief, a biography of Charles V, and moral guides such as the EpÃ®tre d'OthÃ©a, an allegorical advice text drawing on classical and biblical exemplars. Her most notable achievement, Le Livre de la CitÃ© des Dames (1405), systematically refutes misogynistic claims from contemporary literature like Jean de Meun's Roman de la Rose by envisioning a metaphorical city populated by virtuous historical and mythical women, erected with the aid of allegorical figures Reason, Rectitude, and Justice. This work, grounded in empirical examples of women's capabilities rather than abstract ideals, positioned her as a defender of female dignity and intellect in a patriarchal society, influencing later discussions on gender roles. De Pizan retired to a Dominican convent in Poissy later in life, where she likely composed her final pieces, including a poem celebrating Joan of Arc's victories.
